title: ASHA workers: health at the doorstep
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Accredited Social Health Activist links the village and the health system.
body:
When a woman in a village reaches a hospital in time to give birth, or a child gets a vaccine on schedule, there is often an **ASHA** behind it. The word means hope in Hindi, and it also stands for Accredited Social Health Activist. This post looks at who ASHAs are, what they do, how they are paid, how the world recognised them in 2022, and what unions including BMS are asking for.

## Background: a link between village and system

The ASHA was introduced in **2005** under the National Rural Health Mission, now the National Health Mission. The idea was to have, in every village, a woman who could link people to the public health system. Under the scheme's selection norms described in standard references, the ASHA is a woman resident of the village, preferably aged 25 to 45 and educated up to Class 10, though this can be relaxed. She is selected with the involvement of the gram panchayat and is accountable to the community. WHO says there are more than one million ASHAs in India.

## Her tasks

The ASHA's work is wide:

- encouraging **institutional delivery** and accompanying women to hospitals;
- promoting **immunisation**, family planning, nutrition and sanitation;
- home visits for **newborn and child care**;
- screening and follow-up for conditions such as tuberculosis, hypertension and diabetes;
- keeping village health records and acting as a depot holder for supplies such as oral rehydration salts, iron and folic acid tablets and contraceptives;
- during the COVID-19 pandemic, **surveys, tracing and awareness**, often at personal risk.

WHO's description of her role runs from maternal care and child immunisation to tuberculosis, communicable disease control and health promotion on nutrition, sanitation and healthy living.

## How she is paid

ASHAs have not been given a salary. The Health Ministry says a fixed monthly incentive of Rs 2,000 applies across the country for routine and recurring activities, along with performance-based incentives for specific tasks under national health programmes. In September 2022 the Government approved additional incentives, and States may add their own, so the actual amount differs from State to State. Since the launch of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, ASHAs can also earn team-based incentives of up to Rs 1,000 a month, linked to monitored performance indicators. In September 2018 the Prime Minister announced that the regular incentive would be doubled, and the Government also extended free life and accident insurance.

Beyond money, the Ministry lists non-monetary support, including a uniform, an identity card, a mobile phone, a drug kit and a rest room, and a cash award of Rs 20,000 with a citation for those who leave after at least ten years of service.

## Social security: what exists

The Ministry's note on the 2018 benefit package says ASHAs are covered by:

- **Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana**, Rs 2 lakh on death, with the Centre paying the premium;
- **Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana**, Rs 2 lakh for accidental death or permanent disability and Rs 1 lakh for partial disability, again with the premium paid by the Centre;
- **PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan**, a pension of Rs 3,000 a month after age 60, with the premium shared equally by the Centre and the beneficiary.

The Interim Budget speech for 2024-25 also extended Ayushman Bharat health cover of Rs 5 lakh a year to all ASHAs.

## The 2022 recognition

On 22 May 2022, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced the **Global Health Leaders Awards** at the opening session of the 75th World Health Assembly. India's ASHAs were among six recipients, honoured for their role in linking communities to the health system. Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated them, saying they are at the forefront of ensuring a healthy India. The recognition shows how important their work is. Unions have used the occasion to argue that recognition should be matched by worker status at home.

## What unions seek

The Indian Labour Conference's 45th session in May 2013 recommended that scheme workers be recognised as workers, with minimum wages and social security. ASHAs fall in that group. Union demands include:

- a **fixed monthly wage**, not only incentives that depend on tasks;
- **social security**, pension and insurance as a matter of right;
- proper **uniforms, transport and equipment**;
- **timely payment** of incentives, since delays hit the poorest workers hardest.

## The BMS position

BMS has raised the ASHA's cause alongside that of Anganwadi and other scheme workers. At its rally at Jantar Mantar on 11 December 2023, it demanded that scheme workers be recognised as workers, with EPF, ESI, gratuity and pension, a fair promotion policy and a raise in salaries for NHM workers among others. In its pre-Budget letter of 6 January 2025, it asked for recognition of ASHA, Anganwadi, NHM and mid-day meal workers as workers and said that honoraria should be raised since the last increase was in 2018.

## What remains to be done

Several questions remain open:

- Will the fixed component be raised and linked to a wage standard, or will the model remain mostly task-based?
- Will States match the Centre in paying incentives on time?
- Will the 2022 Supreme Court reasoning on Anganwadi gratuity be extended to ASHAs through law or court orders? That judgment concerned Anganwadi workers only, so the answer is not automatic.
- Will the social security schemes listed above reach every ASHA in practice, with enrolment checked at district level?

## Closing

ASHAs are often described as the foot soldiers of public health. The task of making ASHAs workers in law, with the dignity and security that goes with it, remains, and a movement that stands for *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit* has good reason to keep pressing for it.
